title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
hook: past the Himalayas, in a sea of sand, Draupadi falls, and Yudhishthira does not turn around
carry: she loved Arjuna more than the rest of us
tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday the Pandavas' last journey began: ornaments off at the gate, a dog following, and Arjuna's bow thrown back into the sea. Your line was each step is lighter. What did you set down for an hour? Day eight hundred seventy-four.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `THE BOW GOES INTO THE SEA.`

segments.voice: Seven travelers climb into the Himalayas: five brothers, one queen, one dog. They cross the mountains and, beyond them, a great desert of sand, and far off they can see Meru, the mountain at the center of the world. They're walking in single file, with Yudhishthira in front, and Draupadi near the back. Then, without warning, she drops to the ground. Bhima sees her fall. And the man at the front of the line keeps walking. Today, the first of the travelers falls, and someone asks why.
screen: `OVER THE MOUNTAINS.` → `A DESERT OF SAND, MERU AHEAD.` → `DRAUPADI FALLS.`

segments.voice: Bhima calls out to his elder brother. In Ganguli's telling, his question is simple: she never did anything wrong, so why has she fallen? Yudhishthira answers without stopping. She loved Arjuna more than the rest of us, he says. That is what she is paying for now. And he walks on, the text says, without looking at her. That's a hard sentence to sit with. Draupadi has been at the center of so much of this story. She was married to all five brothers. She was dragged into the dice hall and humiliated, and asked the question that shamed the whole hall. She lost her sons in the night raid. And at the end of the road, this is the reason given for her fall: that her heart leaned toward one husband. Readers argue about this moment, and the epic doesn't settle it. Some hear Yudhishthira giving a strict, almost bookkeeping answer, the logic of the road: each falls by a small flaw, and nothing is hidden. Some notice that he never actually stops walking, never kneels, and ask what that costs him. And some point out that the epic isn't finished with this scene. Draupadi's fall is not the last word on Draupadi. We'll see her again. For now, there's just a line of travelers getting shorter, and a question asked by the brother who stopped to look. Bhima turns back to the path. The dog keeps walking.
screen: `BHIMA: "WHY HAS SHE FALLEN?"` · `"SHE LOVED ARJUNA MORE"` · `HE WALKS ON WITHOUT LOOKING` · then, large: `THE EPIC DOESN'T SETTLE IT`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who has been with you on a long stretch of road, and who isn't anymore, for any reason. Breathe in and say their name silently. Breathe out and, instead of walking on, stop. Stay with them for a few breaths, the way Bhima stopped to look. You don't need to explain why they left the road. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi. The queen of the five brothers, who falls first on the last journey, in the sea of sand beyond the mountains.
Your line: she loved Arjuna more than the rest of us. Today, when someone falls behind, be the one who stops to ask about them. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Draupadi's fall on the last journey is told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva; Hindu readers and storytellers often discuss Yudhishthira's explanation, and Draupadi is honored in many retellings and in temple traditions of her own.

fork.setup: you're Bhima, walking behind Draupadi. she falls in the sand, and your brother at the front doesn't stop. what do you do?
options: call out and ask why she fell.
stay with her and stop walking.
fork.reveal: Bhima asks why; Yudhishthira answers that she loved Arjuna more, and walks on without looking back.

original.note: Draupadi: the queen of the five brothers, the first to fall on the last journey.

trapdoor: what you thought: Draupadi falls because the journey is too hard.
what it means: Yudhishthira gives a reason: her heart leaned toward Arjuna.
what a scholar hears: readers argue over this verdict, and the epic brings Draupadi back later.
